The shepherds and their people are warned (verses 1–3)

Henry understands these figurative words as predicting the destruction of Jerusalem and of the Jewish church and nation, later plainly foretold by Jesus as the time approached.

If even mighty cedars fall, how can lesser fir trees imagine they will stand?

When wise and godly people fall into sin, or influential and wealthy people fall into trouble, their downfall warns those with fewer advantages.

A nation is in a sad condition when people who ought to be its shepherds behave instead like young lions.

The pride of the Jordan was the thick vegetation along its banks.

When floods covered the banks, lions emerged roaring.

In Henry's application, Jerusalem's destruction should therefore warn other churches.

The Good Shepherd and the two staffs (verses 4–14)

Henry explains these words as announcing Christ's coming in judgment to a Jewish nation and religious community that had become deeply corrupt.

People whose minds are darkened may do wrong while justifying themselves.

But God does not pronounce innocent those who approve their own wrongdoing.

How can we ask God to bless dishonest methods of gaining wealth, or thank him for the profits of such conduct?

The community had experienced serious religious decline but failed to recognize it.

The Good Shepherd would care for his flock, giving special attention to the poor.

The prophet appears to have used two staffs.

The first, Beauty, represented the Jewish nation's privileges within its national covenant.

The second, Bands, represented the unity that had held the flock together.

Yet many preferred false teachers.

Worldly-mindedness and friendship with sin place people in hostility to God.

The prophet requested his wages and was paid thirty pieces of silver.

By divine direction, he threw them to the potter, rejecting the sum as a contemptible price.

Henry interprets this as foreshadowing Judas's bargain to betray Christ and the later use of the money.

Nothing ruins a people more surely than the collapse of their mutual bonds of fellowship.

As sin increases, love grows cold, and disagreements turn into public conflict.

People who have provoked God against themselves should not be surprised if they begin to fight one another.

Deliberate contempt for Christ brings ruin.

If professing Christians properly valued him, they would not quarrel so fiercely over trivial matters.

The foolish shepherd abandons the flock (verses 15–17)

Having shown what happens when the Good Shepherd's care is rejected, the vision shows the further misery of people abused by foolish shepherds.

Henry relates the portrait to the scribes and Pharisees as Jesus described them.

Such leaders do nothing to uphold the weak or encourage those who are discouraged.

They look only for personal comfort while treating the flock cruelly.

An idol shepherd may dress and appear like a true shepherd, receive submission and enjoy generous support.

Yet through neglect or wicked example, the shepherd lets the sheep perish.

Henry says this pattern fits leaders in many churches and nations, while interpreting the prophecy as having a particularly severe application to some Jewish teachers.

Those who deceive others toward destruction will themselves receive severe condemnation.
classic_reading:
[Zech.11.1-Zech.11.3]
Chapter 11
Chapter Outline
Destruction to come upon the Jews. | (1-3) |
The Lord's dealing with the Jews. | (4-14) |
The emblem and curse of a foolish shepherd. | (15-17) |
Verses 1-3
In figurative expressions, that destruction of Jerusalem, and of the Jewish church and nation, is foretold, which our Lord Jesus, when the time was at hand, prophesied plainly and expressly. How can the fir trees stand, if the cedars fall? The falls of the wise and good into sin, and the falls of the rich and great into trouble, are loud alarms to those every way their inferiors. It is sad with a people, when those who should be as shepherds to them, are as young lions. The pride of Jordan was the thickets on the banks; and when the river overflowed the banks, the lions came up from them roaring. Thus the doom of Jerusalem may alarm other churches.
[Zech.11.4-Zech.11.14]
Verses 4-14
Christ came into this world for judgment to the Jewish church and nation, which were wretchedly corrupt and degenerate. Those have their minds wofully blinded, who do ill, and justify themselves in it; but God will not hold those guiltless who hold themselves so. How can we go to God to beg a blessing on unlawful methods of getting wealth, or to return thanks for success in them? There was a general decay of religion among them, and they regarded it not. The Good Shepherd would feed his flock, but his attention would chiefly be directed to the poor. As an emblem, the prophet seems to have taken two staves; Beauty, denoted the privileges of the Jewish nation, in their national covenant; the other he called Bands, denoting the harmony which hitherto united them as the flock of God. But they chose to cleave to false teachers. The carnal mind and the friendship of the world are enmity to God; and God hates all the workers of iniquity: it is easy to foresee what this will end in. The prophet demanded wages, or a reward, and received thirty pieces of silver. By Divine direction he cast it to the potter, as in disdain for the smallness of the sum. This shadowed forth the bargain of Judas to betray Christ, and the final method of applying it. Nothing ruins a people so certainly, as weakening the brotherhood among them. This follows the dissolving of the covenant between God and them: when sin abounds, love waxes cold, and civil contests follow. No wonder if those fall out among themselves, who have provoked God to fall out with them. Wilful contempt of Christ is the great cause of men's ruin. And if professors rightly valued Christ, they would not contend about little matters.
[Zech.11.15-Zech.11.17]
Verses 15-17
God, having showed the misery of this people in their being justly left by the Good Shepherd, shows their further misery in being abused by foolish shepherds. The description suits the character Christ gives of the scribes and Pharisees. They never do any thing to support the weak, or comfort the feeble-minded; but seek their own ease, while they are barbarous to the flock. The idol shepherd has the garb and appearance of a shepherd, receives submission, and is supported at much expense; but he leaves the flock to perish through neglect, or leads them to ruin by his example. This suits many in different churches and nations, but the warning had an awful fulfilment in the Jewish teachers. And while such deceive others to their ruin, they will themselves have the deepest condemnation.

God protects his people (verses 1–8)

God's prophecy announces a heavy burden for the enemies of his church, but comfort and blessing for Israel.

The Lord will confuse their plans and weaken their courage.

Henry admits the precise meaning is unclear.

Yet God often begins by calling the poor and despised, and even the weakest may become like David, courageous and excellent in all that is good.

May the labor and example of Christians be like fire among dry wood or a torch in a sheaf, spreading divine love and true religion on every side.

The Spirit leads people to mourn over Christ (verses 9–14)

The prophet describes a day when God defends and delivers Jerusalem.

When Christ first came, he wounded the serpent's head and broke the dark powers opposing his kingdom.

At his second coming, he will complete their defeat and bring down all hostile powers.

Death itself will be swallowed up in victory.

The Holy Spirit is gracious and merciful, the source of holiness and every spiritual grace.

He is also the Spirit of supplication, showing people their ignorance, need, guilt, misery and danger, and teaching them to pray.

Henry interprets this prophecy as anticipating a time when the Jews would recognize Jesus as the crucified Messiah.

They would look toward him with faith and mourn for him, in public and privately, with each person grieving personally.

There is a holy sorrow over sin that flows from the Spirit's work.

Such sorrow strengthens faith in Christ and prepares people to rejoice in God.

It is evidence of genuine grace and prayer.

That pattern applies to everyone who mourns over sin with godly sorrow.

Looking to Christ crucified moves the heart to repent of the sin for which he suffered.
classic_reading:
[Zech.12.1-Zech.12.8]
Chapter 12
Chapter Outline
Punishment of the enemies of Judah. | (1-8) |
Repentance and sorrow of the Jews. | (9-14) |
Verses 1-8
Here is a Divine prediction, which will be a heavy burden to all the enemies of the church. But it is for Israel; for their comfort and benefit. It is promised that God will make foolish the counsels, and weaken the courage of the enemies of the church. The exact meaning is not clear; but God often begins by calling the poor and despised; and in that day even the feeblest will resemble David, and be as eminent in courage and every thing good. Desirable indeed is it that the examples and labours of Christians should render them as fire among wood, as a torch in a sheaf, to kindle the flame of Divine love, to spread religion on the right hand and on the left.
[Zech.12.9-Zech.12.14]
Verses 9-14
The day here spoken of, is the day of Jerusalem's defence and deliverance, that glorious day when God will appear for the salvation of his people. In Christ's first coming he bruised the serpent's head, and broke all the powers of darkness that fought against God's kingdom among men. In his second coming he will complete their destruction, when he shall put down all opposing rule, principality, and power; and death itself shall be swallowed up in that victory. The Holy Spirit is gracious and merciful, and is the Author of all grace or holiness. He, also, is the Spirit of supplications, and shows men their ignorance, want, guilt, misery, and danger. At the time here foretold, the Jews will know who the crucified Jesus was; then they shall look by faith to him, and mourn with the deepest sorrow, not only in public, but in private, even each one separately. There is a holy mourning, the effect of the pouring out of the Spirit; a mourning for sin, which quickens faith in Christ, and qualifies for joy in God. This mourning is a fruit of the Spirit of grace, a proof of a work of grace in the soul, and of the Spirit of supplications. It is fulfilled in all who sorrow for sin after a godly sort; they look to Christ crucified, and mourn for him. Looking by faith upon the cross of Christ will cause us to mourn for sin after a godly sort.

The fountain opened for sin (verses 1–6)

A fountain would be opened to the rulers and people of the Jews for cleansing from sin.

Henry identifies it as Christ's atoning blood united with his sanctifying grace.

He understands the fountain as having been closed to unbelieving Israel but expects it to be opened to the people when the Spirit of grace humbles and softens their hearts.

The opened fountain is the pierced side of Christ.

We are all unclean because of sin.

Yet a fountain is open to wash us, and its streams of mercy continually flow.

Christ's blood, and the pardoning mercy of God made known through the new covenant, will never be exhausted.

This fountain is available to every believer.

Those who believe in Christ are his spiritual offspring, part of the family of David and members of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Through his grace, Christ removes the dominion of sin, even the sins to which the heart clings most strongly.

People cleansed through this fountain are both justified and sanctified.

They turn away from love of the world and from the desires of sinful flesh, the two great idols, to cling to God alone.

Henry sees a complete reformation following his anticipated conversion of Israel to Christ.

False prophets would recognize their guilt and folly and return to proper work.

When we realize we have strayed from duty, genuine repentance brings us back to that duty.

We should accept correction from friends who have helped expose our errors, even if that correction wounds our pride (Proverbs 27:6).

Above all, remember the wounds of our Savior.

He has often been wounded by professing friends and even genuine disciples when their conduct contradicts his word.

The Shepherd is struck and a remnant is saved (verses 7–9)

Henry understands this passage as a prophecy of the suffering and death of Christ.

God the Father commanded the sword of his justice to rise against his Son when the Son willingly offered his soul for sin.

Because Christ is truly God, the Father calls him “my Fellow.”

The Son and the Father are one.

He is the Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.

As a sacrifice, he had to be slain; without bloodshed there is no remission of sins.

He had no sin of his own for which to answer.

The prophecy may encompass all his suffering, especially his agony in the garden and upon the cross, where he endured deep anguish until divine justice was satisfied.

When the Shepherd was struck, the sheep were scattered.

Jesus himself connected these words to the disciples' flight on the night of his betrayal.

Henry sees further application in the destruction of corrupt and hypocritical elements within the professing church.

He also identifies Roman judgment upon many Jews following the rejection and crucifixion of Jesus and opposition to the gospel.

That is Henry's historical and theological interpretation, not a newly established fact about Jewish people.

Yet a remnant was to be saved.

God would refine his people like gold.

He would be their God, and the ultimate result of their trials would be praise, honor and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ.
classic_reading:
[Zech.13.1-Zech.13.6]
Chapter 13
Chapter Outline
The Fountain for the remission of sins, The conviction of the false prophets. | (1-6) |
The death of Christ, and the saving of a remnant of the people. | (7-9) |
Verses 1-6
In the time mentioned at the close of the foregoing chapter, a fountain would be opened to the rulers and people of the Jews, in which to wash away their sins. Even the atoning blood of Christ, united with his sanctifying grace. It has hitherto been closed to the unbelieving nation of Israel; but when the Spirit of grace shall humble and soften their hearts, he will open it to them also. This fountain opened is the pierced side of Christ. We are all as an unclean thing. Behold a fountain opened for us to wash in, and streams flowing to us from that fountain. The blood of Christ, and God's pardoning mercy in that blood, made known in the new covenant, are a fountain always flowing, that never can be emptied. It is opened for all believers, who as the spiritual seed of Christ, are of the house of David, and, as living members of the church, are inhabitants of Jerusalem. Christ, by the power of his grace, takes away the dominion of sin, even of beloved sins. Those who are washed in the fountain opened, as they are justified, so they are sanctified. Souls are brought off from the world and the flesh, those two great idols, that they may cleave to God only. The thorough reformation which will take place on the conversion of Israel to Christ, is here foretold. False prophets shall be convinced of their sin and folly, and return to their proper employments. When convinced that we are gone out of the way of duty, we must show the truth of our repentance by returning to it again. It is well to acknowledge those to be friends, who by severe discipline are instrumental in bringing us to a sight of error; for faithful are the wounds of a friend, [Prov.27.6] Pr 27:6. And it is always well for us to recollect the wounds of our Saviour. Often has he been wounded by professed friends, nay, even by his real disciples, when they act contrary to his word.
[Zech.13.7-Zech.13.9]
Verses 7-9
Here is a prophecy of the sufferings of Christ. God the Father gave order to the sword of his justice to awake against his Son, when he freely made his soul an offering for sin. As God, he is called "my Fellow." Christ and the Father are one. He is the Shepherd who was to lay down his life for the sheep. If a Sacrifice, he must be slain, for without shedding of the life-blood there was no remission. This sword must awake against him, yet he had no sin of his own to answer for. It may refer to the whole of Christ's sufferings, especially his agonies in the garden and on the cross, when he endured unspeakable anguish till Divine justice was fully satisfied. Smite the Shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered. This passage our Lord Jesus declares was fulfilled, when all his disciples, in the night wherein he was betrayed, forsook him and fled. It has, and shall have its accomplishment, in the destruction of the corrupt and hypocritical part of the professed church. Because of the sin of the Jews in rejecting and crucifying Christ, and in opposing his gospel, the Romans would destroy the greater part. But a remnant would be saved. And if we are his people, we shall be refined as gold; he will be God, and the end of all our trials and sufferings will be praise, and honour, and glory, at the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Jerusalem's suffering and the coming of Christ (verses 1–7)

During his earthly life Jesus often stood on the Mount of Olives.

He ascended to heaven from that place, and afterward distress and desolation overtook the Jewish nation.

Henry presents this as one figurative interpretation of the vision.

But he also reports that many understand the prophecy to concern events still unfulfilled, including troubles beyond what we can now fully imagine.

He does not settle this dispute by declaring one reading certain.

Every believer can nevertheless look forward to Christ's coming in power with joy, since the Lord is their God.

For a long time, the church may be weakened and deformed by sin.

Truth and error, happiness and sorrow, may be mixed together.

The same mixture affects each believer: grace and remaining corruption coexist.

But when circumstances are darkest and hope seems most remote, God can bring light.

Deliverance may come just when his people have stopped expecting it.

Living waters and divine judgments (verses 8–15)

Some understand the living waters flowing from Jerusalem as an image of the gospel spreading from that city.

Neither the gospel and its appointed means of grace nor the grace the Holy Spirit works through them can be exhausted.

Persecution's heat, temptation's storms and other painful experiences cannot stop their lasting benefit.

The passage appears also to announce severe judgments against those who oppose the settlement of the Jews in their own land.

Henry insists that events alone can establish how far this language should be interpreted literally.

Human rage and violence are only faint images of the hostility found among those lost in their sins.

Even animals can suffer because human beings sin and bring ruin on the world around them.

Through such judgments, God reveals his displeasure against wickedness.

The holiness of ordinary life in the latter days (verses 16–21)

Henry considers it impossible for all the nations literally to travel to Jerusalem every year to celebrate one festival.

He therefore says this language must be understood figuratively.

The Feast of Tabernacles represents gospel worship.

Every day of a Christian's life is to be lived as a holy celebration.

The Lord's Day, in particular, should receive special devotion.

Those who neglect God's appointed means of grace cannot expect to receive the benefits of fellowship with him.

This neglect becomes its own punishment: by refusing the duty, they lose the privilege.

The passage promises a time of unusual peace and purity for the church.

Ordinary work and holy worship will be governed by the same principles of faith, love and obedience.

Holiness will spread more widely because the Holy Spirit will be poured out more abundantly than before.

Even common things will become holy through their use.

Every action and enjoyment of a believer should be directed toward God's glory.

Our whole life should become one continuous sacrifice of devotion, untouched by selfish motives.

How far the church now is from such purity!

But Henry anticipates days when God will reform and enlarge it.

Still, perfect holiness and perfect happiness are found in heaven alone.
classic_reading:
[Zech.14.1-Zech.14.7]
Chapter 14
Chapter Outline
The sufferings of Jerusalem. | (1-7) |
Encouraging prospects, and the destruction of her enemies. | (8-15) |
The holiness of the latter days. | (16-21) |
Verses 1-7
The Lord Jesus often stood upon the Mount of Olives when on earth. He ascended from thence to heaven, and then desolations and distresses came upon the Jewish nation. Such is the view taken of this figuratively; but many consider it as a notice of events yet unfulfilled, and that it relates to troubles of which we cannot now form a full idea. Every believer, being related to God as his God, may triumph in the expectation of Christ's coming in power, and speak of it with pleasure. During a long season, the state of the church would be deformed by sin; there would be a mixture of truth and error, of happiness and misery. Such is the experience of God's people, a mingled state of grace and corruption. But, when the season is at the worst, and most unpromising, the Lord will turn darkness into light; deliverance comes when God's people have done looking for it.
[Zech.14.8-Zech.14.15]
Verses 8-15
Some consider that the progress of the gospel, beginning from Jerusalem, is referred to by the living waters flowing from that city. Neither shall the gospel and means of grace, nor the graces of the Spirit wrought in the hearts of believers by those means, ever fail, by reason either of the heat of persecution, or storms of temptation, or the blasts of any other affliction. Tremendous judgments appear to be foretold, to be sent upon those who should oppose the settlement of the Jews in their own land. How far they are to be understood literally, events alone can determine. The furious rage and malice which stir up men against each other, are faint shadows of the enmity which reigns among those who have perished in their sins. Even the inferior creatures often suffer for the sin of man, and in his plagues. Thus God will show his displeasure against sin.
[Zech.14.16-Zech.14.21]
Verses 16-21
As it is impossible for all nations literally to come to Jerusalem once a year, to keep a feast, it is evident that a figurative meaning must here be applied. Gospel worship is represented by the keeping of the feast of tabernacles. Every day of a Christian's life is a day of the feast of tabernacles; every Lord's day especially is the great day of the feast; therefore every day let us worship the Lord of hosts, and keep every Lord's day with peculiar solemnity. It is just for God to withhold the blessings of grace from those who do not attend the means of grace. It is a sin that is its own punishment; those who forsake the duty, forfeit the privilege of communion with God. A time of complete peace and purity of the church will arrive. Men will carry on their common affairs, and their sacred services, upon the same holy principles of faith, love and obedience. Real holiness shall be more diffused, because there shall be a more plentiful pouring forth of the Spirit of holiness than ever before. There shall be holiness even in common things. Every action and every enjoyment of the believer, should be so regulated according to the will of God, that it may be directed to his glory. Our whole lives should be as one constant sacrifice, or act of devotion; no selfish motive should prevail in any of our actions. But how far is the Christian church from this state of purity! Other times, however, are at hand, and the Lord will reform and enlarge his church, as he has promised. Yet in heaven alone will perfect holiness and happiness be found.
